On the Aramaizing doubling of the first radical in the <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. תתּם (instead of תתם), vid., Ges. §67, rem. 8, comp. 3. It is translated <hi type="italic">an lucrum</hi> (<hi type="italic">ei</hi>) <hi type="italic">si integras facias vias tuas.</hi> The meaning of the whole strophe is mainly determined according to the rendering of המיּראתך (like המבינתך, <reference osisRef="Job.39.26">Job 39:26</reference>, with Dechî, and as an exception with <hi type="italic">Munach</hi>, not removed to the place of the <hi type="italic">Metheg;</hi> vid., <hi type="italic">Psalter,</hi> ii. 491, Anm. 1). If the suff. is taken objectively (from fear of thee), e.g., Hirz., we have the following line of thought: God is neither benefited by human virtue nor injured by human sin, so that when He corrects the sinner He is turning danger from himself; He neither rewards the godly because He is benefited by his piety, nor punishes the sinner because by his sinning he threatens Him with injury. Since, therefore, if God chastises a man, the reason of it is not to be found in any selfish purpose of God, it must be in the sin of the man, which is on its own account worthy of punishment. But the logical relation in which <reference osisRef="Job.22.5">Job 22:5</reference> stands to <reference osisRef="Job.22.4">Job 22:4</reference> does not suit this: perhaps from fear of thee ... ? no, rather because of thy many and great sins! Does He go (on that account) with thee into judgment? No (it would be absurd to suppose that); therefore thy wickedness must be great (in proportion to the greatness of thy suffering), and thy misdeeds infinitely many. If we now look at what precedes, we shall have to put aside the thought drawn into <reference osisRef="Job.22.2">Job 22:2</reference> and <reference osisRef="Job.22.3">Job 22:3</reference> by Ewald (and also by Hahn): whether God, perhaps with the purpose of gaining greater advantage from piety, seeks to raise it by unjustly decreed suffering; for this thought has nothing to indicate it, and is indeed certainly false, but on account of the force of truth which lies in it (there is a decreeing of suffering for the godly to raise their piety) is only perplexing. <div eID="gen7831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7832" type="x-p"/> First of all, we must inquire how it is that Eliphaz begins his speech thus. All the exhortations to penitence in which the three exhaust themselves, rebound from Job without affecting him. Even Eliphaz, the oldest among them, full of a lofty, almost prophetic consciousness, has with the utmost solicitude allured and terrified him, but in vain. And it is the cause of God which he brings against him, or rather his own well-being that he seeks, without making an impression upon him. Then he reminds him that God is in Himself the all-sufficient One; that no advantage accrues to Him from human uprightness, since His nature, existing before and transcending all created things, can suffer neither diminution nor increase from the creature; that Job therefore, since he remains inaccessible to that well-meant call to penitent humiliation, has refused not to benefit Him, but himself; or, what is the reverse side of this thought (which is not, however, expressed), that he does no injury to Him, only to himself. And yet in what except in Job’s sin should this decree of suffering have its ground? If it is a self-contradiction that God should chastise a man because he fears Him, there must be sin on the side of Job; and indeed, since the nature of the sin is to be measured according to the nature of the suffering, great and measureless sin. This logical necessity Eliphaz now regards as real, without further investigation, by opening out this bundle of sins in the next strophe, and reproaching Job directly with that which Zophar, <reference osisRef="Job.20.19-Job.20.21">Job 20:19-21</reference>, aiming at Job, has said of the רשׁע. entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Job.22.6-Job.9.6">Job 22:6-9   6</reference>  For thou distrainedst thy brother without cause, <div eID="gen7832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7833" type="x-p"/> And the clothes of the naked thou strippedst off.   7  Thou gavest no water to the languishing, <div eID="gen7833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7834" type="x-p"/> And thou refusedst bread to the hungry.   8  And the man of the arm-the land was his, <div eID="gen7834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7835" type="x-p"/> And the honourable man dwelt therein.   9  Thou sentest widows away empty, <div eID="gen7835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7836" type="x-p"/> And the arms of the orphan are broken. <div eID="gen7836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7837" type="x-p"/> The reason of exceeding great suffering most be exceeding great sins. Job must have committed such sins as are here cited; therefore Eliphaz directly attributes guilt to him, since he thinks thus to tear down the disguise of the hypocrite. The strophe contains no reference to the Mosaic law: the compassionate Mosaic laws respecting duties towards widows and orphans, and the poor who pledge their few and indispensable goods, may have passed before the poet’s mind; but it is not safe to infer it from the expression. As specific Mohammedan commandments among the wandering tribes even in the present day have no sound, so the poet dare not assume, in connection with the characters of his drama, any knowledge, of the Sinaitic law; and of this he remains conscious throughout: their standpoint is and remains that of the Abrahamic faith, the primary commands (later called the ten commands of piety, el-felâhh) of which were amply sufficient for stigmatizing that to which this strophe gives prominence as sin. It is only the force of the connection of the matter here which gives the <hi type="italic">futt.</hi> which follow כי a retrospective meaning. חבל is connected either with the accusative of the thing for which the pledge is taken, as in the law, which meets a response in the heart, Exo 22:25.; or with the accus. of the person who is seized, as here אחיך; or, if this is really (as Bär asserts) a mistake that has gained a footing, which has Codd. and old printed editions against it, rather אחיך. lxx, Targ., Syr., and Jer. read the word as plural. ערוּמים (from ערום), like γυμνοί, Jam 2:15, <hi type="italic">nudi</hi> (comp. Seneca, <hi type="italic">de beneficiis,</hi> v. 13: <hi type="italic">si quis male vestitum et pannosum videt, nudum se vidisse dicit</hi>), are, according to our mode of expression, the half-naked, only scantily (vid., <reference osisRef="Isa.20.2">Isa 20:2</reference>) clothed.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Job.22.10-Job.11.10">Job 22:10-11 10</reference>  Therefore snares are round about thee, <div eID="gen7838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7839" type="x-p"/> And fear terrifieth thee suddenly; 11  Or percievest thou not the darkness, <div eID="gen7839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7840" type="x-p"/> And the overflow of waters, which covereth thee? <div eID="gen7840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7841" type="x-p"/> On account of this inhuman mode of action by which he has challenged the punishment of justice, snares are round about him (comp. Bildad’s picture of this fate of the evil-doer, <reference osisRef="Job.18.8-Job.18.10">Job 18:8-10</reference>), destruction encompasses him on every side, so that he sees no way out, and must without any escape succumb to it. And the approaching ruin makes itself known to him time after time by terrors which come suddenly upon him and disconcert him; so that his outward circumstances being deranged and his mind discomposed, he has already in anticipation to taste that which is before him. In <reference osisRef="Job.22.11">Job 22:11</reference>, לא תראה is by no means to be taken as an eventual circumstantial clause, whether it is translated affirmatively: or darkness (covers thee), that thou canst not see; or interrogatively: or does darkness (surround thee), that thou seest not? In both cases the verb in the principal clause is wanting; apart from the new turn, which או introduces, being none, it would then have to be explained with Löwenthal: or has the habit of sinning already so dulled thy feeling and darkened thine eye, that thou canst not perceive the enormity of thy transgression? Job complains of it as being unmerited, and therefore mysterious; Eliphaz, on the other hand, is desirous that he should open his eyes that he may perceive in this darkness of sorrow, this flood of suffering, the well-deserved punishment of his heinous sins, and anticipate the worst by penitence. לא תכסּךּ is a relative clause, and belongs logically also to חשׁך, comp. <reference osisRef="Isa.60.2">Isa 60:2</reference>, where שׁפעת is also found in <reference osisRef="Job.22.6">Job 22:6</reference> (from שׁפע, <hi type="italic">abundare;</hi> comp. Arab. <hi type="italic">šf‛ ,</hi> ספק, <reference osisRef="Job.20.22">Job 20:22</reference>). Eliphaz now insinuates that Job denies the special providence of God, because he doubts the exceptionless, just government of God. In the second strophe he has explained his affliction as the result of his uncharitableness; now he explains it as the result of his unbelief, which is now become manifest.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Job.22.12-Job.14.12">Job 22:12-14 12</reference>  Is not Eloah high as the heavens? <div eID="gen7841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7842" type="x-p"/> See but the head of the stars, how exalted! 13  So then thou thinkest: “What doth God know? <div eID="gen7842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7843" type="x-p"/> Can He judge through the thick cloud? 14  Clouds veil Him that He seeth not, <div eID="gen7843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7844" type="x-p"/> And in the vault of heaven He walketh at His pleasure.” <div eID="gen7844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7845" type="x-p"/> Because Job has denied the distribution of worldly fortune, of outward prosperity and adversity, according to the law of the justice that recompenses like for like, Eliphaz charges him with that unbelief often mentioned in the Psalms (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.11">Psa 73:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.94.7">Psa 94:7</reference>; comp. <reference osisRef="Isa.29.15">Isa 29:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.12">Eze 8:12</reference>), which denies to the God in heaven, as Epicurus did to the gods who lead a blessed life in the spaces between the worlds, a knowledge of earthly things, and therefore the preliminary condition for a right comprehension of them. The mode of expression here is altogether peculiar. גּבהּ שׁמים is not <hi type="italic">acc. loci,</hi> as the like accusatives in combination with the verb שׁכן, <reference osisRef="Isa.57.15">Isa 57:15</reference>, may be taken: the substantival clause would lead one to expect בּגבהּ, or better בּגבהי (<reference osisRef="Job.11.8">Job 11:8</reference>); it is rather (similar to <reference osisRef="Job.11.8">Job 11:8</reference>) <hi type="italic">nomin. praedicati:</hi> Eloah is the height of the heavens = heaven-high, as high as the heavens, therefore certainly highly, and indeed very highly, exalted above this earth. In this sense it is continued with <hi type="italic">Waw explic.:</hi> and behold (= behold then) the head of the stars, that, or how (כּי as in <reference osisRef="Gen.49.15">Gen 49:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.29">1Sa 14:29</reference>, <hi type="italic">quod</hi> = <hi type="italic">quam</hi>) exalted they are. וּראה has <hi type="italic">Asla</hi> (<hi type="italic">Kadma</hi>) in correct texts, and רמו is written רמּוּ (<hi type="italic">râmmu</hi>) with a so-called Dag. <hi type="italic">affectuosum</hi> (Olsh. §83, <hi type="italic">b</hi>). It may be received as certain that ראשׁ, the head (<hi type="italic">vertex</hi>), beside ראה (not ספר), does not signify the sum (Aben-Ezra). But it is questionable whether the genitive that follows ראשׁ is <hi type="italic">gen. partitivus:</hi> the highest among the stars (Ew., Hirz., Schlottm.), or <hi type="italic">gen. epexegeticus:</hi> the head, i.e., (in relation to the rest of the universe) the height, which is formed by the stars, or even which they occupy (Ges. <hi type="italic">coelum stellatum</hi>); the partitive rendering is to be preferred, for the Semitic perception recognises, as the plural שׁמים implies, nearer and more distant celestial spheres. The expression “head of the stars” is therefore somewhat like <hi type="italic">fastigium coeli</hi> (the extreme height, i.e., the middle of the vault of heaven), or <hi type="italic">culmen aereum</hi> (of the aether separating the strata of air above); the summit of the stars rising up into the extremest spheres is intended (we should say: the fixed stars, or to use a still more modern expression, the milky way), as also the רמו naturally refers to ראשׁ כוכבים as one notion (<hi type="italic">summitas astrorum</hi> = <hi type="italic">summa astra</hi>). <div eID="gen7845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7846" type="x-p"/> The connection of what follows with Waw is not adversative (Hirz., Ew., and others: and yet thou speakest), it is rather consecutive (Hahn: and since thou speakest; better: and in consequence of this thou speakest; or: thus speakest thou, thinkest thou then). The undeniable truth that God is exalted, and indeed absolute in His exaltation, is misapplied by Job to the false conclusion: what does God know, or (since the <hi type="italic">perf.</hi> in interrogative sentences frequently corresponds to the Latin conjunctive, vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.11.3">Psa 11:3</reference>) how should God know, or take knowledge, i.e., of anything that happens on earth? In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.22.13">Job 22:13</reference></hi> the potential takes the place of this modal perfect: can He rule judicially behind the dark clouds, i.e., over the world below from which He is shut out? בּעד (of like verbal origin with the Arab. <hi type="italic">b‛da , post,</hi> prop. distance, separation, succession, but of wider use) signifies here, as in <reference osisRef="Job.1.10">Job 1:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.9.7">Job 9:7</reference>, behind, <hi type="italic">pone,</hi> with the secondary notion of being encompassed or covered by that which shuts off. Far from having an unlimited view of everything earthly from His absolute height, it is veiled from His by the clouds, so that He sees not what occurs here below, and unconcerned about it He walks the circle of the heavens (that which vaults the earth, the inhabitants of which seem to Him, according to <reference osisRef="Isa.40.22">Isa 40:22</reference>, as grasshoppers); התלּך is here, after the analogy of <hi type="italic">Kal,</hi> joined with the accus. of the way over which He walks at His pleasure: <hi type="italic">orbem coelum obambulat.</hi> By such unworthy views of the Deity, Job puts himself on a par with the godless race that was swept away by the flood in ancient days, without allowing himself to be warned by this example of punishment.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Job.22.15-Job.18.15">Job 22:15-18 15</reference> Wilt thou observe the way of the ancient world, <div eID="gen7846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7847" type="x-p"/> Which evil men have trodden, 16 Who were withered up before their time, <div eID="gen7847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7848" type="x-p"/> Their foundation was poured out as a stream, 17 Who said unto God: Depart from us! <div eID="gen7848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7849" type="x-p"/> And what can the Almighty do to them? 18 And notwithstanding He had filled their houses with good- <div eID="gen7849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7850" type="x-p"/> The counsel of the wicked be far from me! <div eID="gen7850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7851" type="x-p"/> While in <reference osisRef="Ps.139.24">Psa 139:24</reference> דרך עולם prospectively signifies a way of eternal duration (comp. <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.20">Eze 26:20</reference>, עם עולם, of the people who sleep the interminably long sleep of the grave), ארח עולם signifies here retrospectively the way of the ancient world, but not, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.6.16">Jer 6:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.18.15">Jer 18:15</reference>, the way of thinking and acting of the pious forefathers which put their posterity to shame, but of a godless race of the ancient world which stands out as a terrible example to posterity. Eliphaz asks if Job will observe, i.e., keep (שׁמר as in <reference osisRef="Ps.18.22">Psa 18:22</reference>), this way trodden by people (מתי, comp. אנשׁי, <reference osisRef="Job.34.36">Job 34:36</reference>) of wickedness. Those worthless ones were withered up, i.e., forcibly seized and crushed, ולא־עת, when it was not yet time (ולא after the manner of a circumstantial clause: <hi type="italic">quum nondum,</hi> as <reference osisRef="Ps.139.16">Psa 139:16</reference>), i.e., when according to God’s creative order their time was not yet come. On קמּטוּ,<note placement="foot">This קמטו, according to the Masora, is the middle word of the book of Job (חצי הספר).</note> vid., on <reference osisRef="Job.16.8">Job 16:8</reference>; lxx correctly, συνελήφθησαν ἄωροι, nevertheless συλλαμβάνειν is too feeble as a translation of קמט; for as Arab. <hi type="italic">qbṣ</hi> signifies to take with the tip of the finer, whereas Arab. <hi type="italic">qbḍ</hi> signifies to take with the whole bent hand, so קמט, in conformity to the dull, emphatic final consonant, signifies “to bind firmly together.” In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.22.16">Job 22:16</reference></hi> יוּצק is not <hi type="italic">perf. Pual</hi> for יצּק (Ew. §83, <hi type="italic">b</hi>), for this exchange, contrary to the law of vowels, of the sharp form with the lengthened form is without example; it must at least have been written יוּצּק (comp. Jdg 18:29). It is <hi type="italic">fut. Hoph.,</hi> which, according to <reference osisRef="Job.11.15">Job 11:15</reference>, might be יצּק; here, however, it is with a resolving, not assimilation, of the <hi type="italic">Jod,</hi> as in Lev 21:10. entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Job.22.19-Job.20.19">Job 22:19-20 19</reference>  The righteous see it and rejoice, <div eID="gen7852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7853" type="x-p"/> And the innocent mock at them: 20  “Verily our opponent is destroyed, <div eID="gen7853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7854" type="x-p"/> And the fire hath devoured their abundance.” <div eID="gen7854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7855" type="x-p"/> This thought corresponds to that expressed as a wish, hope, or anticipation at the close of many of the Psalms, that the retributive justice of God, though we may have to wait a long time for it, becomes at length the more gloriously manifest to the joy of those hitherto innocently persecuted, Psa 58:11. entries.content_osis: Job 22:21-25 21  Make friends now with Him, so hast thou peace; <div eID="gen7856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7857" type="x-p"/> Thereby good will come unto thee. 22  Receive now teaching from His mouth, <div eID="gen7857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7858" type="x-p"/> And place His utterances in thy heart. 23  If thou returnest to the Almighty, thou shalt be built up again; <div eID="gen7858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7859" type="x-p"/> If thou puttest away iniquity far from thy tents. 24  And lay by in the dust the gold ore, <div eID="gen7859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7860" type="x-p"/> And under the pebbles of the brooks the gold of Ophir. 25  So shall the Almighty be to thee gold ore in abundance, <div eID="gen7860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7861" type="x-p"/> And silver to thee of the brightest lustre. <div eID="gen7861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7862" type="x-p"/> The relationship of the verbs סכן, שׁכן, and Arab. <hi type="italic">sakana ,</hi> has been already discussed on <reference osisRef="Job.22.2">Job 22:2</reference> : the <hi type="italic">Hiph.</hi> signifies to be on friendly terms with any one; to enter into, or to stand in, an intimate relationship to any one (<reference osisRef="Ps.139.3">Psa 139:3</reference>); then also (as the Greek φιλεῖν) to get accustomed to, to be used to (Num 22:30). The second <hi type="italic">imper.</hi> is consecutive, as e.g., <reference osisRef="Prov.3.4">Pro 3:4</reference> : and have as the result of it peace (Arab. <hi type="italic">fa'âslam</hi>) = so shalt thou have peace, Ges. §130, 2.
